title: CTS Parables of the Bible — Unit 2: The Song of the Vineyard

blocks.en: 🍇 Parables of the Bible — Unit 2: The Song of the Vineyard
blocks.es_reference: 🍇 Las Parábolas de la Biblia — Unidad 2: El Canto de la Viña

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "What more could have been done to My vineyard that I have not done in it?" — Isaiah 5:4 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "¿Qué más se podía hacer a mi viña, que yo no haya hecho en ella?" — Isaías 5:4 (RVG)

blocks.en: Orientation
blocks.es_reference: Orientación

blocks.en: Imagine owning a comfortable apartment overlooking the ocean. Friends are traveling through the area, and you tell them they may stay there at no charge. The cupboards are full and the rooms are furnished, and you ask only one thing: please clean up when you leave. When you return, the sink is full of dirty dishes, food is rotting on the counter, and the carpet is stained. When you ask about it, your friends tell you they resented being asked to clean up. You gave them everything and asked for almost nothing in return. How would you feel?
blocks.es_reference: Imagine que usted es dueño de un apartamento cómodo con vista al mar. Unos amigos van a pasar por esa zona, y usted les dice que pueden quedarse allí sin costo. Las alacenas están llenas y los cuartos están amueblados, y usted pide una sola cosa: por favor, limpien antes de irse. Cuando usted regresa, el fregadero está lleno de platos sucios, la comida se pudre sobre el mostrador y la alfombra está manchada. Cuando usted pregunta, sus amigos le dicen que les molestó que les pidiera limpiar. Usted les dio todo y pidió casi nada a cambio. ¿Cómo se sentiría?

blocks.en: That is very nearly the feeling of Isaiah 5:1–7, the Song of the Vineyard. It is the Old Testament parable that stands closest to the teaching of Jesus, because Jesus deliberately retold it in His parable of the tenants (Matthew 21:33–46). If we understand Isaiah's song, we will hear Jesus' parable the way His first listeners heard it. In Unit 1 we saw that a parable is an earthly story with a heavenly meaning, that it disarms the listener, and that it often leads him to pronounce judgment on himself. Isaiah's song does all three, and it does them in only seven verses.
blocks.es_reference: Ese es casi exactamente el sentimiento de Isaías 5:1–7, el Canto de la Viña. Es la parábola del Antiguo Testamento más cercana a la enseñanza de Jesús, porque Jesús la volvió a contar a propósito en Su parábola de los labradores malvados (Mateo 21:33–46). Si entendemos el canto de Isaías, oiremos la parábola de Jesús como la oyeron Sus primeros oyentes. En la Unidad 1 vimos que una parábola es una historia terrenal con un significado celestial, que desarma al oyente y que a menudo lo lleva a pronunciar juicio contra sí mismo. El canto de Isaías hace las tres cosas, y las hace en solo siete versículos.

blocks.en: I. The Setting
blocks.es_reference: I. El contexto

blocks.en: Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem in the eighth century before Christ, during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (Isaiah 1:1). The song in chapter 5 most likely comes from the early years of his ministry, when Judah was enjoying prosperity. Trade was growing, the wealthy were building fine houses, and the temple services continued without interruption. From the outside, everything looked healthy. But chapter 1 has already told us what God saw: hands full of offerings and hands full of blood (Isaiah 1:11–15). Religion was busy while justice was dying.
blocks.es_reference: Isaías profetizó en Jerusalén en el siglo octavo antes de Cristo, durante los reinados de Uzías, Jotam, Acaz y Ezequías (Isaías 1:1). El canto del capítulo 5 probablemente viene de los primeros años de su ministerio, cuando Judá disfrutaba de prosperidad. El comercio crecía, los ricos construían casas finas y los servicios del templo continuaban sin interrupción. Desde fuera, todo parecía sano. Pero el capítulo 1 ya nos ha dicho lo que Dios veía: manos llenas de ofrendas y manos llenas de sangre (Isaías 1:11–15). La religión estaba ocupada mientras la justicia moría.

blocks.en: Into that setting Isaiah steps forward, perhaps at a harvest festival when songs about vineyards were common, and announces that he will sing a love song. "Now let me sing to my Well-beloved a song of my Beloved regarding His vineyard" (Isaiah 5:1). The crowd leans in. A vineyard in the Song of Solomon and in the love poetry of the ancient world often pictured a bride. The listeners expect a romance. What they receive is a lawsuit.
blocks.es_reference: En ese contexto Isaías se pone de pie, quizás en una fiesta de la cosecha cuando los cantos sobre viñas eran comunes, y anuncia que va a cantar un canto de amor: "Ahora cantaré a mi amado el cantar de mi amado a su viña" (Isaías 5:1). La multitud se inclina para escuchar. En el Cantar de los Cantares y en la poesía de amor del mundo antiguo, la viña a menudo representaba a una novia. Los oyentes esperan un romance. Lo que reciben es un pleito.

blocks.en: II. The Care of the Owner (Isaiah 5:1–2)
blocks.es_reference: II. El cuidado del dueño (Isaías 5:1–2)

blocks.en: The first verses describe everything the owner did. He chose "a very fruitful hill." He dug the ground and cleared it of stones, which in the hill country of Judah was backbreaking work. He planted it with "the choicest vine," the Hebrew soreq, a vine of the finest quality. He built a watchtower in the middle of it so that he could guard it from thieves and animals, and he hewed a winepress out of the rock, a sign that he fully expected a harvest. Nothing was left undone. Every provision for fruitfulness had been made.
blocks.es_reference: Los primeros versículos describen todo lo que hizo el dueño. Escogió "una ladera muy fértil". Cavó la tierra y la limpió de piedras, lo cual en la región montañosa de Judá era un trabajo agotador. La plantó con "vides escogidas", en hebreo soreq, una vid de la mejor calidad. Edificó una torre en medio de ella para guardarla de ladrones y animales, y labró un lagar en la roca, señal de que esperaba plenamente una cosecha. No quedó nada por hacer. Se había provisto todo lo necesario para que diera fruto.

blocks.en: This is grace before demand. The owner does not ask for grapes and then leave the vine to fend for itself. He prepares, protects, and provides first, and only then does he look for fruit. Israel's story followed the same order. God brought a vine out of Egypt, cleared the land before it, and planted it (Psalm 80:8–9). He gave His people the covenant, the law, the land, the temple, the priesthood, and the prophets. Everything Israel was, it had received.
blocks.es_reference: Esto es gracia antes que exigencia. El dueño no pide uvas y luego deja la vid a su suerte. Primero prepara, protege y provee, y solo entonces busca fruto. La historia de Israel siguió el mismo orden. Dios sacó una vid de Egipto, limpió la tierra delante de ella y la plantó (Salmo 80:8–9). Dio a Su pueblo el pacto, la ley, la tierra, el templo, el sacerdocio y los profetas. Todo lo que Israel era, lo había recibido.

blocks.en: Then comes the turn: "He expected it to bring forth good grapes, but it brought forth wild grapes." The Hebrew word be'ushim describes grapes that are sour, shriveled, even rotten and foul-smelling. It is not that the vineyard produced nothing. It produced something worse than nothing: fruit that was useless for wine and offensive to the owner who had given it everything.
blocks.es_reference: Entonces viene el giro: "esperaba que diese uvas, y dio uvas silvestres". La palabra hebrea be'ushim describe uvas agrias, arrugadas, incluso podridas y malolientes. No es que la viña no produjera nada. Produjo algo peor que nada: fruto inútil para el vino y ofensivo para el dueño que se lo había dado todo.

blocks.en: III. The Question of the Owner (Isaiah 5:3–4)
blocks.es_reference: III. La pregunta del dueño (Isaías 5:3–4)

blocks.en: Now the singer's voice changes. The owner himself speaks, and he turns to the audience. "And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge, please, between Me and My vineyard" (Isaiah 5:3). This is the method we saw with Nathan and David in Unit 1: a juridical parable. The listeners are invited to sit as the jury in a case they do not yet realize is about themselves. Any fair-minded person in the crowd would agree that the owner had been wronged.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora cambia la voz del cantor. El dueño mismo habla, y se dirige a los oyentes: "Ahora, pues, vecinos de Jerusalén y varones de Judá, juzgad ahora entre mí y mi viña" (Isaías 5:3). Este es el método que vimos con Natán y David en la Unidad 1: una parábola judicial. Se invita a los oyentes a sentarse como jurado en un caso que todavía no saben que trata de ellos. Cualquier persona justa entre la multitud estaría de acuerdo en que el dueño había sido agraviado.

blocks.en: Then comes the heartbreaking question: "What more could have been done to My vineyard that I have not done in it? Why then, when I expected it to bring forth good grapes, did it bring forth wild grapes?" (Isaiah 5:4). These are not the words of a distant landlord. They are the words of a grieved lover who has given everything. The question has no answer, and that is the point. There was nothing more he could have done.
blocks.es_reference: Luego viene la pregunta que parte el corazón: "¿Qué más se podía hacer a mi viña, que yo no haya hecho en ella? ¿Cómo, esperando yo que diese uvas, ha dado uvas silvestres?" (Isaías 5:4). Estas no son palabras de un propietario distante. Son las palabras de un amante herido que lo ha dado todo. La pregunta no tiene respuesta, y ese es el punto. No había nada más que él pudiera haber hecho.

blocks.en: Interpreters from different traditions weigh this verse differently, and students should know the conversation. Arminian and Wesleyan interpreters often cite Isaiah 5:4 as a clear example of grace that is real and sufficient yet resisted: God did everything needed for fruit, and the failure lay entirely with the vineyard. Reformed interpreters generally read the verse as describing the outward privileges God gave the covenant nation as a whole, which leaves the nation without excuse, rather than a statement about the inner working of grace in individual hearts. Both agree on the main thrust. The fault was not in the owner, and Judah had no excuse.
blocks.es_reference: Intérpretes de distintas tradiciones valoran este versículo de manera diferente, y los estudiantes deben conocer la conversación. Los intérpretes arminianos y wesleyanos a menudo citan Isaías 5:4 como un ejemplo claro de una gracia real y suficiente que, sin embargo, es resistida: Dios hizo todo lo necesario para que hubiera fruto, y la falla estuvo enteramente en la viña. Los intérpretes reformados generalmente leen el versículo como una descripción de los privilegios externos que Dios dio a la nación del pacto en su conjunto, los cuales dejan a la nación sin excusa, y no como una afirmación sobre la obra interior de la gracia en cada corazón. Ambos coinciden en lo principal. La culpa no estaba en el dueño, y Judá no tenía excusa.

blocks.en: IV. The Verdict of the Owner (Isaiah 5:5–6)
blocks.es_reference: IV. El veredicto del dueño (Isaías 5:5–6)

blocks.en: Having asked the jury to decide, the owner announces his own sentence. He will take away its hedge so that it is eaten, break down its wall so that it is trampled, and lay it waste. It will not be pruned or dug, and briers and thorns will come up. Then he adds a sentence no human farmer could ever say: "I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain on it" (Isaiah 5:6). At that moment the audience knows. Only one Owner commands the clouds. This is no ordinary vineyard, and this is no ordinary farmer.
blocks.es_reference: Después de pedir al jurado que decida, el dueño anuncia su propia sentencia. Quitará su vallado para que sea consumida, derribará su cerca para que sea hollada y la dejará desierta. No será podada ni cavada, y crecerán el cardo y los espinos. Luego añade una frase que ningún agricultor humano podría decir: "aun a las nubes mandaré que no derramen lluvia sobre ella" (Isaías 5:6). En ese momento la audiencia lo sabe. Solo un Dueño manda a las nubes. Esta no es una viña común, y este no es un agricultor común.

blocks.en: The judgment is fitting. God does not so much add a punishment as remove His protection. The hedge and the wall had been gifts; now the vineyard will have what it seemed to want, a life without the Owner's care. Judgment in Scripture often looks like this. God gives people over to what they have chosen (Romans 1:24–28).
blocks.es_reference: El juicio es adecuado. Dios no tanto añade un castigo como retira Su protección. El vallado y la cerca habían sido regalos; ahora la viña tendrá lo que parecía querer, una vida sin el cuidado del Dueño. En la Escritura, el juicio a menudo se ve así. Dios entrega a las personas a lo que han escogido (Romanos 1:24–28).

blocks.en: It is worth saying plainly that God's patience is great but it is not endless. We sometimes speak as though God's mercy and patience are infinite in the sense that they never come to an end. God is indeed merciful and patient beyond anything we deserve, but Scripture also speaks of a day when patience gives way to judgment. The vineyard had been cared for, visited, and warned. There came a day when the Owner said, "Enough."
blocks.es_reference: Vale la pena decir claramente que la paciencia de Dios es grande, pero no es interminable. A veces hablamos como si la misericordia y la paciencia de Dios fueran infinitas en el sentido de que nunca llegan a su fin. Dios en verdad es misericordioso y paciente mucho más allá de lo que merecemos, pero la Escritura también habla de un día en que la paciencia da paso al juicio. La viña había sido cuidada, visitada y advertida. Llegó el día en que el Dueño dijo: "Basta".

blocks.en: V. The Meaning Revealed (Isaiah 5:7)
blocks.es_reference: V. El significado revelado (Isaías 5:7)

blocks.en: Now Isaiah names the parable plainly: "For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are His pleasant plant. He looked for justice, but behold, oppression; for righteousness, but behold, a cry for help" (Isaiah 5:7). The jury has convicted itself.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora Isaías nombra la parábola claramente: "Ciertamente la viña de Jehová de los ejércitos es la casa de Israel, y los hombres de Judá planta deliciosa suya. Esperaba juicio, y he aquí vileza; justicia, y he aquí clamor" (Isaías 5:7). El jurado se ha condenado a sí mismo.

blocks.en: The final lines contain one of the most powerful wordplays in the Old Testament. God looked for mishpat, justice, and found mispach, bloodshed or oppression. He looked for tsedaqah, righteousness, and heard tse'aqah, the cry of the oppressed. The words sound almost alike, just as wild grapes look almost like good ones from a distance. Judah's society had the outward shape of a godly nation, but the fruit was the opposite of what God wanted. The cry of the poor, the widow, and the cheated worker was rising to heaven.
blocks.es_reference: Las últimas líneas contienen uno de los juegos de palabras más poderosos del Antiguo Testamento. Dios buscaba mishpat, justicia, y halló mispach, derramamiento de sangre u opresión. Buscaba tsedaqah, rectitud, y oyó tse'aqah, el clamor del oprimido. Las palabras suenan casi igual, así como las uvas silvestres parecen casi buenas desde lejos. La sociedad de Judá tenía la forma externa de una nación piadosa, pero el fruto era lo contrario de lo que Dios quería. El clamor del pobre, de la viuda y del trabajador defraudado subía al cielo.

blocks.en: Notice what fruit God was seeking. He did not say He looked for more sacrifices, larger festivals, or better attendance at the temple. He looked for justice and righteousness: right relationships with God expressed in fair and merciful treatment of other people. The fruit God wants from His people is a changed life that blesses others.
blocks.es_reference: Note qué fruto buscaba Dios. No dijo que buscaba más sacrificios, fiestas más grandes o mejor asistencia al templo. Buscaba justicia y rectitud: relaciones correctas con Dios expresadas en un trato justo y misericordioso hacia los demás. El fruto que Dios quiere de Su pueblo es una vida transformada que bendice a otros.

blocks.en: VI. The Wild Grapes Named (Isaiah 5:8–30)
blocks.es_reference: VI. Las uvas silvestres nombradas (Isaías 5:8–30)

blocks.en: The rest of chapter 5 names the wild grapes in a series of woes. Woe to those who join house to house and field to field until there is no room for anyone else (vv. 8–10), the greed that swallowed the land of small farmers. Woe to those who rise early to chase strong drink and whose feasts have music but no thought for the work of the LORD (vv. 11–12). Woe to those who drag sin along "as if with a cart rope" and mock God's warnings (vv. 18–19). "Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil" (v. 20), who reverse God's moral order. Woe to those wise in their own eyes (v. 21). Woe to those who are heroes at drinking and who acquit the guilty for a bribe while taking justice from the righteous (vv. 22–23).
blocks.es_reference: El resto del capítulo 5 nombra las uvas silvestres en una serie de ayes. ¡Ay de los que juntan casa a casa y añaden heredad a heredad hasta que no queda lugar para nadie más (vv. 8–10), la avaricia que se tragó la tierra de los pequeños agricultores! ¡Ay de los que se levantan de mañana para seguir la bebida y cuyos banquetes tienen música pero ningún pensamiento para la obra de Jehová (vv. 11–12)! ¡Ay de los que arrastran el pecado como con coyundas de carreta y se burlan de las advertencias de Dios (vv. 18–19)! "¡Ay de los que a lo malo dicen bueno, y a lo bueno malo!" (v. 20), que invierten el orden moral de Dios. ¡Ay de los sabios en sus propios ojos (v. 21)! ¡Ay de los valientes para beber, que justifican al impío por soborno y quitan la justicia al justo (vv. 22–23)!

blocks.en: These woes turn the parable into a mirror. Greed, pleasure without God, mocking conscience, moral confusion, pride, and corrupt justice are not only sins of ancient Judah. They grow in every generation and in every church. A pastor preaching Isaiah 5 does not need to invent applications. He only needs to hold the mirror steady.
blocks.es_reference: Estos ayes convierten la parábola en un espejo. La avaricia, el placer sin Dios, la burla de la conciencia, la confusión moral, el orgullo y la justicia corrupta no son solo pecados del antiguo Judá. Crecen en cada generación y en cada iglesia. El pastor que predica Isaías 5 no necesita inventar aplicaciones. Solo necesita sostener firme el espejo.

blocks.en: VII. The Vineyard Across Scripture
blocks.es_reference: VII. La viña a lo largo de la Escritura

blocks.en: The vineyard becomes one of the great images of the Bible. Psalm 80 prays for the vine brought out of Egypt whose walls have been broken down. Jeremiah hears God say, "I had planted you a noble vine" (Jeremiah 2:21), and Hosea calls Israel a luxuriant vine that bears fruit for itself (Hosea 10:1). But Isaiah himself does not leave the vineyard in ruins. In Isaiah 27:2–6 he sings a second vineyard song, this time a song of restoration: the LORD keeps His vineyard, waters it every moment, and one day "Israel shall blossom and bud, and fill the face of the world with fruit." Judgment is not God's last word.
blocks.es_reference: La viña llega a ser una de las grandes imágenes de la Biblia. El Salmo 80 ora por la vid sacada de Egipto cuyos vallados han sido derribados. Jeremías oye a Dios decir: "Te planté de vid escogida" (Jeremías 2:21), y Oseas llama a Israel una vid frondosa que da fruto para sí misma (Oseas 10:1). Pero Isaías mismo no deja la viña en ruinas. En Isaías 27:2–6 canta un segundo canto de la viña, esta vez un canto de restauración: Jehová guarda Su viña, la riega en todo momento, y un día "florecerá y echará renuevos Israel, y la faz del mundo llenará de fruto". El juicio no es la última palabra de Dios.

blocks.en: When Jesus told the parable of the tenants, He opened with the details of Isaiah 5: a landowner planted a vineyard, set a hedge around it, dug a winepress, and built a tower (Matthew 21:33). Every listener in the temple courts recognized the song. But Jesus added a new element. In Isaiah the problem was the vineyard's fruit; in Jesus' parable the problem is the tenants, the leaders who refused to give the owner his fruit and finally killed his son. We will study that parable in Unit 13.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Jesús contó la parábola de los labradores, comenzó con los detalles de Isaías 5: un padre de familia plantó una viña, la cercó de vallado, cavó en ella un lagar y edificó una torre (Mateo 21:33). Todo oyente en los atrios del templo reconoció el canto. Pero Jesús añadió un elemento nuevo. En Isaías el problema era el fruto de la viña; en la parábola de Jesús el problema son los labradores, los líderes que se negaron a dar al dueño su fruto y finalmente mataron a su hijo. Estudiaremos esa parábola en la Unidad 13.

blocks.en: And in John 15 Jesus declares, "I am the vine, you are the branches" (John 15:5). Where Israel failed to bear fruit, Jesus Himself is the true and faithful Vine. We do not bear fruit by trying harder to be a better vineyard; we bear fruit by abiding in Him. Donald Grey Barnhouse loved to point to the Great Vine at Hampton Court near London, planted in 1768 and still producing grapes more than two and a half centuries later. It grows from a single root, and its branches stretch far from the main stem, yet they bear fruit because the life of the vine flows through them. Careful pruning keeps it fruitful. So Jesus says, "every branch that bears fruit He prunes, that it may bear more fruit" (John 15:2).
blocks.es_reference: Y en Juan 15 Jesús declara: "Yo soy la vid, vosotros los pámpanos" (Juan 15:5). Donde Israel no dio fruto, Jesús mismo es la Vid verdadera y fiel. No damos fruto esforzándonos más por ser una mejor viña; damos fruto permaneciendo en Él. A Donald Grey Barnhouse le gustaba señalar la Gran Vid de Hampton Court, cerca de Londres, plantada en 1768 y que todavía produce uvas más de dos siglos y medio después. Crece de una sola raíz, y sus pámpanos se extienden lejos del tronco principal, y aun así dan fruto porque la vida de la vid fluye por ellos. Una poda cuidadosa la mantiene fructífera. Así dice Jesús: "todo aquel que lleva fruto, lo limpiará, para que lleve más fruto" (Juan 15:2).

blocks.en: VIII. Preaching the Song of the Vineyard
blocks.es_reference: VIII. Cómo predicar el Canto de la Viña

blocks.en: A simple outline follows the movement of the text. First, the care of the Owner (vv. 1–2): God has done everything needed for fruit in our lives. Second, the question of the Owner (vv. 3–4): what more could He have done? Third, the verdict of the Owner (vv. 5–7): God looks for fruit, and He will not wait forever. The preacher may close with the hope of Isaiah 27 and John 15, that the vineyard can yet bear fruit through the true Vine.
blocks.es_reference: Un bosquejo sencillo sigue el movimiento del texto. Primero, el cuidado del Dueño (vv. 1–2): Dios ha hecho todo lo necesario para que haya fruto en nuestras vidas. Segundo, la pregunta del Dueño (vv. 3–4): ¿qué más pudo haber hecho? Tercero, el veredicto del Dueño (vv. 5–7): Dios busca fruto, y no esperará para siempre. El predicador puede concluir con la esperanza de Isaías 27 y Juan 15: la viña todavía puede dar fruto por medio de la Vid verdadera.

blocks.en: One illustration drives home the law of fruitfulness. Farmers in one region once decided to eat their big potatoes and save the small ones for seed. After years of this, their potatoes had shrunk to the size of marbles. They learned that you cannot keep the best for yourself and plant the leftovers; the harvest reflects the planting. "Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7). Many Christians give God the leftovers of their time, money, and love, and then wonder why their lives bear so little fruit.
blocks.es_reference: Una ilustración grabará la ley de la fructificación. En cierta región, unos agricultores decidieron comerse las papas grandes y guardar las pequeñas para semilla. Después de años de hacerlo, sus papas se habían reducido al tamaño de canicas. Aprendieron que no se puede guardar lo mejor para uno mismo y sembrar las sobras; la cosecha refleja la siembra. "Todo lo que el hombre sembrare, eso también segará" (Gálatas 6:7). Muchos cristianos le dan a Dios las sobras de su tiempo, su dinero y su amor, y luego se preguntan por qué sus vidas dan tan poco fruto.

blocks.en: We must also be careful how we measure fruit. Fruit is found first in faithfulness, not always in quick results. A missionary in Urfa, in old Mesopotamia, labored thirteen years before he baptized a single convert. Then a cholera epidemic struck, and the people fled in panic, leaving the sick and dying behind. The missionary stayed, caring for the sufferers tenderly and tirelessly until he himself caught the disease and died. The survivors carried his body to a grove outside the city walls, and it seemed his work had ended. But when his successor arrived, a large crowd met him miles from the city and brought him in with honor. Many turned to Christ, and a church was built in memory of "the man who died for us." The grain of wheat had fallen into the ground, and the harvest came (John 12:24). The Owner of the vineyard sees fruit that we may not live to see.
blocks.es_reference: También debemos tener cuidado de cómo medimos el fruto. El fruto se encuentra primero en la fidelidad, no siempre en resultados rápidos. Un misionero en Urfa, en la antigua Mesopotamia, trabajó trece años antes de bautizar a un solo convertido. Entonces llegó una epidemia de cólera, y la gente huyó en pánico, dejando atrás a los enfermos y moribundos. El misionero se quedó, cuidando a los que sufrían con ternura y sin descanso, hasta que él mismo contrajo la enfermedad y murió. Los sobrevivientes llevaron su cuerpo a una arboleda fuera de los muros de la ciudad, y parecía que su obra había terminado. Pero cuando llegó su sucesor, una gran multitud salió a recibirlo a varios kilómetros de la ciudad y lo llevó con honores. Muchos se volvieron a Cristo, y se construyó una iglesia en memoria de "el hombre que murió por nosotros". El grano de trigo había caído en la tierra, y vino la cosecha (Juan 12:24). El Dueño de la viña ve fruto que tal vez nosotros no vivamos para ver.

blocks.en: Finally, the vineyard reminds us why God blesses His people at all. God told Abraham, "I will bless you... and you shall be a blessing" (Genesis 12:2). Judah enjoyed the blessing but forgot the second half of the promise. The church can make the same mistake. The vineyard was never planted for its own enjoyment. It was planted to bear fruit for the Owner, fruit that blesses the world around it.
blocks.es_reference: Por último, la viña nos recuerda por qué Dios bendice a Su pueblo. Dios le dijo a Abraham: "te bendeciré... y serás bendición" (Génesis 12:2). Judá disfrutó la bendición pero olvidó la segunda mitad de la promesa. La iglesia puede cometer el mismo error. La viña nunca se plantó para su propio disfrute. Se plantó para dar fruto para el Dueño, fruto que bendice al mundo que la rodea.

blocks.en: Closing
blocks.es_reference: Conclusión

blocks.en: Isaiah's song begins as a love song, and at its heart it still is one. The Owner who asks, "What more could I have done?" is not a cold landlord. He is a lover who has given everything. The same love would one day send the Son to the vineyard, and that Son would become the true Vine in whom we bear fruit. The question for every reader of Isaiah 5 is simple: when the Owner comes looking for fruit in my life, what will He find?
blocks.es_reference: El canto de Isaías comienza como un canto de amor, y en el fondo sigue siéndolo. El Dueño que pregunta "¿Qué más pude haber hecho?" no es un propietario frío. Es un amante que lo ha dado todo. Ese mismo amor un día enviaría al Hijo a la viña, y ese Hijo llegaría a ser la Vid verdadera en quien damos fruto. La pregunta para todo lector de Isaías 5 es sencilla: cuando el Dueño venga buscando fruto en mi vida, ¿qué encontrará?

mc.stem: In the orientation, the apartment illustration pictures an owner who:
options: Charged his friends a high rent
Gave everything and asked for very little in return
Refused to let anyone use his home
mc.why: Like the vineyard owner, the host provided everything and was repaid with ingratitude.

mc.stem: Isaiah introduces the Song of the Vineyard as:
options: A love song about his Beloved's vineyard
mc.why: The listeners expected a romance, but the love song turned into a lawsuit.

mc.stem: According to this unit, Judah at the time of this song was:
options: Prosperous and religious outwardly while justice was dying
mc.why: Trade grew and temple services continued, but hands full of offerings were also full of blood (Isaiah 1).

mc.stem: Which of these did the owner do for his vineyard (Isaiah 5:2)?
options: Cleared the stones, planted the choicest vine, and built a tower and winepress
mc.why: Every provision for fruitfulness had been made; nothing was left undone.

mc.stem: The unit calls the order of verses 1–2 "grace before demand" because:
options: The owner prepared, protected, and provided before looking for fruit
The owner demanded grapes before planting
The owner never expected any fruit
The vineyard paid for its own care
mc.why: God gave Israel the covenant, law, land, temple, and prophets first; everything Israel was, it had received.

mc.stem: The Hebrew word be'ushim, translated "wild grapes," describes grapes that are:
options: Sour, shriveled, even rotten and foul-smelling
mc.why: The vineyard produced something worse than nothing: fruit useless for wine and offensive to the owner.

mc.stem: In Isaiah 5:3, the owner invites the people of Jerusalem and Judah to:
options: Judge between him and his vineyard
mc.why: This is a juridical parable: the listeners sit as a jury in a case about themselves.

mc.stem: The question "What more could have been done to My vineyard?" shows that:
options: The owner had neglected the vineyard
The fault was not in the owner; there was nothing more he could have done
The owner wanted advice from the crowd
mc.why: The question has no answer, which is the point; it is the grief of a lover who has given everything.

mc.stem: How do Arminian and Wesleyan interpreters often use Isaiah 5:4?
options: As proof that grace is irresistible
As a promise that Judah would never be judged
As a verse about the end times only
As an example of real, sufficient grace that was resisted
mc.why: Reformed interpreters read it as outward covenant privileges; both agree the fault was not the owner's.

mc.stem: What detail in verse 6 reveals that the owner is God?
options: He commands the clouds not to rain on it
He sells the grapes at market
mc.why: Only one Owner commands the clouds; no human farmer could say this.

mc.stem: According to this unit, the judgment in verses 5–6 is fitting because God:
options: Adds a harsh new punishment unrelated to the sin
Removes His protection and gives the vineyard over to what it chose
mc.why: The hedge and wall had been gifts; now the vineyard has life without the Owner's care (compare Romans 1:24–28).

mc.stem: What does this unit teach about God's patience?
options: It never ends under any circumstances
God has no patience at all
It is great but not endless; a day comes when patience gives way to judgment
Patience applies only to the Gentiles
mc.why: God is patient beyond what we deserve, but the vineyard came to a day when the Owner said, "Enough."

mc.stem: In Isaiah 5:7, the vineyard is identified as:
mc.why: The vineyard is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are His pleasant plant.

mc.stem: The wordplay mishpat / mispach contrasts:
mc.why: God looked for mishpat, justice, and found mispach, oppression; the words sound almost alike.

mc.stem: According to this unit, the fruit God looked for in His vineyard was:
options: Justice and righteousness in how people treated one another
mc.why: God wanted right relationships with Him expressed in fair and merciful treatment of others.

mc.stem: "Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil" (Isaiah 5:20) describes:
options: People who give generously to the poor
People who reverse God's moral order
mc.why: This woe is one of the wild grapes Isaiah names after the parable.

mc.stem: Isaiah 27:2–6 is important to this unit because it:
options: Repeats the judgment word for word
Describes the building of the temple
Sings a second vineyard song of restoration
mc.why: In Isaiah 27 the LORD keeps and waters His vineyard, and Israel will fill the world with fruit; judgment is not God's last word.

mc.stem: How does Jesus' parable of the tenants differ from Isaiah's song?
options: Isaiah's song has tenants but no owner
In Isaiah the problem is the fruit; in Jesus' parable the problem is the tenants who kill the son
mc.why: Jesus opens with Isaiah's details (hedge, winepress, tower) but adds tenants and the owner's son.

mc.stem: In John 15, Jesus presents Himself as:
options: The true Vine in whom we bear fruit
mc.why: Where Israel failed to bear fruit, Jesus is the faithful Vine; we bear fruit by abiding in Him.

mc.stem: The potato illustration teaches that:
options: You cannot keep the best for yourself and plant the leftovers; the harvest reflects the planting
God does not care about harvests
mc.why: Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap (Galatians 6:7).

sa.prompt: Describe the setting of Isaiah 5 and explain why Isaiah began with a love song.
sa.model: Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem during the reigns of Uzziah and the kings after him, likely during a time of prosperity when temple services continued but justice was dying. He may have sung at a harvest festival. He began with a love song because a vineyard often pictured a bride, so the crowd expected a romance and leaned in, only to find the song become a lawsuit against them.

sa.prompt: List what the owner did for his vineyard and explain the idea of "grace before demand."
sa.model: The owner chose a very fruitful hill, cleared the stones, planted the choicest vine, built a tower, and hewed a winepress. He prepared, protected, and provided before he looked for any fruit. That is grace before demand: Israel likewise received the covenant, law, land, temple, and prophets before God asked for fruit, so everything Israel had, it had received.

sa.prompt: Explain how Isaiah 5:3–4 works as a juridical parable, connecting it to Nathan and David.
sa.model: In verse 3 the owner asks the people of Jerusalem and Judah to judge between him and his vineyard. Like David hearing Nathan's story, they sit as a jury in a case they do not realize is about themselves. Any fair listener would agree the owner was wronged when he asks what more he could have done, and when verse 7 names the vineyard, they have convicted themselves.

sa.prompt: Present the Arminian/Wesleyan and Reformed readings of Isaiah 5:4 fairly, and state what both agree on.
sa.model: Arminian and Wesleyan interpreters often cite Isaiah 5:4 as grace that was real and sufficient yet resisted: God did everything needed for fruit and the failure lay with the vineyard. Reformed interpreters generally read it as the outward privileges God gave the covenant nation, which left it without excuse, rather than a statement about inner grace in each heart. Both agree the fault was not in the owner and Judah had no excuse.

sa.prompt: Explain the judgment of Isaiah 5:5–6, how verse 6 reveals the owner, and what the unit teaches about God's patience.
sa.model: The owner removes the hedge and breaks down the wall so the vineyard is trampled and overrun with briers and thorns. He then commands the clouds not to rain, which only God can do, revealing the owner's identity. The judgment fits because God removes His protection and gives the vineyard what it chose. God's patience is great but not endless; a day came when the Owner said, "Enough."

sa.prompt: Explain the Hebrew wordplay in Isaiah 5:7 and what it shows about the fruit God wanted.
sa.model: God looked for mishpat, justice, and found mispach, bloodshed or oppression; He looked for tsedaqah, righteousness, and heard tse'aqah, a cry of the oppressed. The words sound almost alike, just as wild grapes can look like good ones from a distance. The fruit God wanted was not more sacrifices or festivals but justice and righteousness in how people treated one another.

sa.prompt: Name at least four of the woes in Isaiah 5:8–23 and explain how they function as a mirror.
sa.model: Isaiah pronounces woe on those who join house to house in greed, who chase strong drink and pleasure without God, who drag sin as with a cart rope and mock God's warnings, who call evil good and good evil, who are wise in their own eyes, and who take a bribe to acquit the guilty. These are the wild grapes. They act as a mirror because the same sins grow in every generation and church.

sa.prompt: Trace the vineyard image through Scripture, including Isaiah 27, Matthew 21, and John 15.
sa.model: Psalm 80, Jeremiah 2, and Hosea 10 also picture Israel as God's vine. Isaiah 27 sings a second vineyard song of restoration, so judgment is not God's last word. In Matthew 21 Jesus retells Isaiah 5 but adds tenants who kill the owner's son. In John 15 Jesus is the true Vine: where Israel failed, He is faithful, and we bear fruit by abiding in Him.

sa.prompt: Explain the lesson of the Hampton Court vine and the potato illustration for a Christian's fruitfulness.
sa.model: The Great Vine at Hampton Court grows from a single root, yet branches far from the stem bear fruit because the vine's life flows through them, and careful pruning keeps it fruitful, as Jesus says in John 15. The potato farmers ate the big potatoes and planted the small ones until their crop shrank to marbles. You cannot keep the best for yourself and plant leftovers; whatever a man sows he reaps (Galatians 6:7).

sa.prompt: Give a preaching outline for Isaiah 5:1–7 and explain how Genesis 12:2 applies the parable to the church.
sa.model: The outline follows the text: the care of the Owner in verses 1–2, the question of the Owner in verses 3–4, and the verdict of the Owner in verses 5–7, closing with the hope of Isaiah 27 and John 15. God told Abraham He would bless him so that he would be a blessing. Judah enjoyed the blessing and forgot the second half, and the church can too; the vineyard exists to bear fruit that blesses others.
